newsitem.title: USA: Worm's long-life gene has implications for humans.
newsitem.headline: Worm's long-life gene has implications for humans.

text.p: A gene that governs the lifespan of a tiny worm has implications for longevity in humans and may hold the key to fighting diabetes, a geneticist said on Friday.

The unpreposessing worm C. elegans, barely visible with the naked eye, can either live fast and die young while times are lush or go into a slow mode of virtual hibernation to conserve energy to get through a lean period.

The worm's pace of life is governed by a gene which is strikingly similar to a human gene that determines how the body uses insulin, according to Gary Ruvkun, whose research into the matter was published in Friday's edition of the journal Science.

"One of the interesting things about this discovery is that it actually endorses a lot of what's been done in aging research in vertebrates," Ruvkun said in a telephone interview from Boston, where he is affiliated with Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard University.
This previous research indicates that a near-starvation diet works with genetic factors to lengthen life, notably in laboratory rats and mice, but also quite possibly in humans, Ruvkun said.
Earlier research has shown that cutting down on calorie intake can increase longevity in laboratory animals by as much as 40 percent, he said.
However, Ruvkun said he and his fellow authors were more excited about the gene's possible impact on the treatment of diabetes, which afflicts about 5 percent of the world's population.

"Two prime genes from the worm are very likely to be involved in human diabetes and we know exactly what the DNA sequence of the worm genes is and we can compare that to the emerging human genome sequence," Ruvkun said.
Researchers at three U.S. laboratories, including Ruvkun's, have discovered many genes in worms with so-called insulin receptor genes which govern metabolism.

When worm food is scarce, low levels of insulin compel C. elegans to store what it eats as fat rather than to fuel growth or reproduction, and this shift in metabolism may cause the increased longevity.

The worm's genetic make-up is similar enough to that in humans to offer effective ways to study how insulin is regulated. Insufficient secretion or utilization of insulin is a prime characteristic of diabetes.
Any new diabetes medication based on Ruvkun's genetic research is at least 10 years away, he said.
